    Diagnostics

    Import / Export

    Save your work to a small text file, or load one back in.

    What to export

    How it works

    Everything happens inside your browser, on your own device. Your score and audio are never uploaded.

    Your files stay with you

    When you add a PDF or an audio file, your browser reads it into this tab’s memory. Nothing is sent to a server, and closing the tab clears it. The only things fetched from the internet are the PDF tools and the fonts the page uses, including any font you pick for the credits.

    Your score

    PDF.js, from Mozilla, draws each page. The PDF Editor keeps your changes as a list of instructions on top of the original, so your original PDF is never changed. Export PDF builds a new file from that list and keeps the pages as sharp vector artwork; pages you cleaned or leveled are drawn from the original scan.

    How the PDF Editor works

    Open the PDF Editor by clicking the score’s name at the top of the settings. It changes your pages without touching the original file. Tick the pages you want, then press a tool’s button: each tool works only on ticked pages. In Clean, Re-kilter and Crop, the button on a page’s corner opens it large, to see it before and after.

    Arrange

    Drag pages to reorder them, and click a page to leave it out. Insert puts a blank page, or another PDF, where you choose. A blank page is the same size as the page before it.

    Clean

    Whitens the paper and removes specks. The paper is measured block by block, so a shadow near the spine or a tinted corner is leveled out. White pushes the paper to white, and Page color levels it to the scan’s own paper tone. Specks takes out small dark dots that touch nothing else; staff lines, notes and staccato dots stay. Revert puts the pages back.

    Re-kilter

    Straightens crooked scans. It looks at the dark ink and tries small turns and bends, keeping whatever makes the staff lines sharpest; bar lines and stems show how far the page is slanted. If the best fit isn’t clearly better than the page as it is, the page is left alone. A crop you already made follows the leveled page.

    Crop

    Finds where the music is and draws each page’s frame before you press it. Scanner lids, shadows, hole punches and dust near the edges are ignored, while a title or page number well inside the page is kept. Each page gives every page its own frame, and Same size gives them all one frame that covers all the music. Auto sets the frames for you, with a Margin for room around the music (never past the page edge), while Manual lets you drag a frame yourself.

    Split spreads

    Finds the gutter between two pages scanned side by side. Split cuts there, so each becomes its own page.

    Re-size

    Pick a paper size, then press Re-size to fit every page to it.

    Watermark

    Tick the pages that should have it and press Watermark to print your text across them. Ticking a page or changing the text then updates the pages at once, and Remove takes it off. It looks the same in the video, the thumbnails and the exported PDF.

    Export PDF

    Builds a new file from your changes while you keep working.

    Your audio

    Your browser decodes the audio and the waveform is measured on your device. Trim, fades, normalize and gain are applied the same way when you listen and when you export. WAV files are written directly, and M4A files are encoded by your browser’s built-in AAC encoder. A long recording is kept in your browser’s private file storage and worked on in pieces, so it never has to fit in memory all at once.

    How the Audio Editor works

    Open the Audio Editor by clicking the audio’s name at the top of the settings. It changes your sound without touching the original file. Its modules are listed on the left; open one to see its controls.

    Pipeline

    Sound runs through the modules from top to bottom: Noise reduction, Spectra, EQ and Imager (drag a light onto another to swap their order), then Fades and Level. The limiter in Level always comes last. A lit module is doing something, and the cable shows the path. Bypass takes out only the module that is open, and Match gain plays the bypassed sound at the loudness of the processed one, so a louder version never just sounds better.

    Noise reduction

    Learn noise from a stretch with only hiss in it. Auto picks that stretch from the whole recording, while Manual lets you pick it. Natural judges the sound in short slices: longer for the lows and mids, so notes can be told apart from the hiss between them, and shorter for the highs (above ~4kHz), so no hiss opens up ahead of a note. Classic is the earlier method. Mains hum finds a steady 50 or 60Hz hum and its overtones, and removes just those with very narrow notches before Noise reduction runs. Noise only plays only what is being taken out.

    Spectra

    Press Draw, then mark a Box, a Band or a Moment on the spectrogram. Heal fills it in from the sound around it. Reduce turns it down. Each edit affects only the slices near it.

    EQ

    Bands can be bells, shelves, or high and low cuts at 12, 24 or 48dB per octave. Each band works on Stereo, Mid or Side. A Dynamic band reacts to how loud its own frequencies are, so a harsh note is turned down only when it is loud. Listen plays only the frequencies a band works on. Auto gain cancels what the curve adds or removes overall, so the volume stays the same. EQ Match measures the average sound of this recording and a reference, and fits bands to the difference.

    Imager

    Width changes how wide the stereo picture is, overall or in three frequency bands. Balance evens out left and right. Center low notes makes the bass below the frequency you pick the same in both ears. Listen plays the middle or the sides alone, and the meter shows how alike the two sides are.

    Level

    Gain makes it louder or quieter. Normalize sets the volume to a target: Loudness uses the integrated loudness (ITU-R BS.1770, as in EBU R128) and ignores silence and quiet stretches, and Peak uses the true peak. Limiter looks 5ms ahead and lowers each moment just enough to stay under the ceiling, counting the peaks between samples, so an encoder or a speaker never clips.

    Fades

    Fades the start in and the end out, with a length and a shape you can set for each.

    Emulator (beta)

    Emulate measures another recording’s tone, the width of each of three frequency bands, and its loudness, then sets your EQ curve, the Imager’s widths and Level’s target to move toward it, as one undo step. Amount says how far.

    Undo and History

    Each editor keeps its own steps. History lists them by name, and you can go back to any one. In the main view, it also lists what the PDF Editor and the Audio Editor changed.

    Page turns

    Each turn is drawn with WebGL, the graphics your browser uses for 3D. The page bends, casts a shadow and turns on your graphics hardware, timed entirely by the turns you set. Drag a turn into its neighbor and it pushes the neighbor along, keeping the least gap, until the video’s start or end stops it. Hold Shift and click turns to select several, or drag a box across the track to select the ones inside it. Dragging a selected turn moves them all together, and clicking empty track clears the selection. Turns to end packs every turn after the playhead against the end of the video at the least gap (before the credits turn, if there are credits) and marks them as still to place, as one undo step. Add page turn then places them in order. In Single page layout every page is its own turn, centered in the frame at the largest size that fits; a turned page either peels away to the left or swings over and fades, as you choose with Turn style, and the credits get a centered card of their own. Changing the layout spaces the turns evenly again, as one undo step.

    Your video

    Every frame is rendered and encoded by your browser. With a sound, the audio is stored losslessly (24-bit) and the video is packed into a MOV file. Real-time recording is the exception: it compresses the audio, and its file is MP4 or WebM. If your browser can’t encode fast enough, it records the preview in real time instead.

    Saved settings

    Your settings are remembered in this browser only. Import and Export save them to a small text file that you keep.

    Support

    glisscore is free, open source, and made by one person (a composer who should probably be writing music).

    If it’s useful to you and you’d like to help cover hosting and upkeep, you can buy me a coffee on Ko-fi.

    There’s no pressure: supporting unlocks nothing, and the app is the same for everyone.
